title: The consonants
hookLine: a tissue held to a kid's lips jumps when she says dhamma right
tomorrow: namo tassa: homage to him. so why not just say his name?

cards: Sunday morning, a temple hall, a row of kids cross-legged on the carpet. The teacher holds a tissue an inch from one girl's lips. Say dhamma.
Damma, she says. The tissue hangs still. Again, says the teacher, with the breath.
Dhamma. This time the tissue jumps, the whole row laughs, and the girl grins like she just won something. That jump is the answer to yesterday's question.
The h in dhamma isn't a letter you hear by itself. It's breath, and you can feel it.

teach.h: PLAIN AND BREATHY: D AND DH.
teach.b: Pali writes breath into the spelling. Many of its consonants come in pairs: a plain sound, and the same sound with a puff of air. k and kh. g and gh. t and th. d and dh. p and ph. b and bh.
The h never stands alone; it rides on the letter before it. Two surprises hide there.

teach.h: TH IS NOT THINK. PH IS NOT PHONE.
teach.b: Pali th is never the th of think: it's a t with breath behind it. And ph is never the f of phone: it's a p with a puff.
Now say Buddha. On the page there's a d, then a dh. The first one holds; the second lets the breath go.
The same breath opens dhamma, and bhagavato, the word that follows namo tassa in the homage.

teach.h: A DOT BENEATH: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.
teach.b: Then there's a second family: sounds made with the tip of the tongue curled back toward the roof of the mouth. In roman letters they wear a small dot underneath.
Tipitaka, the three baskets of the canon, has both kinds of t in one word: the first with the tongue at the teeth, the second curled back. English leaves breath and tongue to chance.
Pali spells them out, so a chanter reading the page knows where the breath goes.
A breath in the word, written down so it isn't lost.

how: Pali chanting books in roman letters write the breathy consonants with an h and mark the tongue-curled ones with a dot beneath; new chanters learn them by ear, chanting along with monks and longtime lay chanters.

o: the silent letters chanters skip to keep pace
the hard sounds only monks learn to say aloud
the plain, breathy and curled sounds of Pali

p: a d with a puff of breath
a t with breath, never the th of think
a p with a puff, never an f

s: the h in dhamma is silent
it's a puff of breath riding on the d; hold your palm up and you can feel it.
Pali ph sounds like the f in phone
it's a p with a puff of air after it, never an f.
a dot under t, d or n marks a tongue-curled sound
in roman letters, the dot beneath means the tip of the tongue curls back toward the roof of the mouth.

games.q: you're lettering a chant poster and the h's are crowding your design: dhamma, Buddha, bhagavato. what do you cut?
o: nothing: each h tells the chanter where a breath goes.
the h's: they're silent, so the chant sounds the same.
every other h: chanters will pick up the pattern.
games.why: the h isn't decoration. dh, bh and the rest are breathy sounds, and the spelling is how a chanter reading the page knows to breathe them.

practice: Hold your palm an inch from your lips. Say damma, plain, and then dhamma, with the breath, and feel the small puff land on your hand.
Go back and forth slowly a few times, then let the hand rest in your lap and sit with the breath that was in the word all along.

wordCard.voice: The consonants. Plain ones and breathy ones, like d and dh, and the tongue-curled ones that carry a dot beneath. Word three of a little Pali.

orig.note: dhamma in Devanagari letters: ध is the breathy dh, written as one letter, not d plus h.

carryVoice: The line for today: a breath in the word, the h you feel more than hear. Day three of the block, done.
